purpose: Add eight more source-exact Isaac Watts hymn stanzas for preaching, devotion, and presentation slides.

defaults.author: Isaac Watts
defaults.rightsBasis: Project Gutenberg identifies this edition as public domain in the USA; the stanza is verified against the stored text.

entries.title: A strait and thorny road
entries.text:
True, 'tis a strait and thorny road,
And mortal spirits tire and faint;
But they forget the mighty God
That feeds the strength of every saint.
entries.slideText:
But they forget the mighty God
That feeds the strength of every saint.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed encouragement for weary believers after explaining God's sustaining strength from Scripture.
entries.reviewNote: This is poetic application. Avoid minimizing exhaustion or suffering, and let the cited KJV passages govern the promise.

entries.title: How strong thine arm
entries.text:
How strong thine arm is, mighty God,
Who would not fear thy Name!
Jesus, how sweet thy graces are!
Who would not love the Lamb!
entries.slideText:
Jesus, how sweet thy graces are!
Who would not love the Lamb!
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed worship stanza in messages about the song of Moses and the Lamb.
entries.reviewNote: The stanza is devotional poetry. Establish Christ's person and worthiness directly from the cited KJV passages.

entries.title: Our Prophet and our King
entries.text:
He has done more than Moses did,
Our Prophet and our King;
From bonds of hell he freed our souls,
And taught our lips to sing.
entries.slideText:
Our Prophet and our King;
From bonds of hell he freed our souls
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed Christ-exalting stanza while showing from Scripture how Christ surpasses Moses.
entries.reviewNote: The comparison is a poetic summary. Explain it carefully from Hebrews and avoid making the hymn the doctrinal authority.

entries.title: He showed our feet the way
entries.text:
Thence he arose, ascending high,
And shew'd our feet the way;
Up to the Lord our flesh shall fly
At the great rising day.
entries.slideText:
Thence he arose, ascending high,
And shew'd our feet the way
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed resurrection stanza in Easter, funeral, or future-hope preaching.
entries.reviewNote: The language is poetic. Teach bodily resurrection and Christ's ascension from the cited KJV passages.

entries.title: Here at thy cross
entries.text:
Here at thy cross, my dying God,
I lay my soul beneath thy love,
Beneath the droppings of thy blood,
Jesus, nor shall it e'er remove.
entries.slideText:
Here at thy cross, my dying God,
I lay my soul beneath thy love
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed response stanza after a clear biblical explanation of Christ's atoning blood.
entries.reviewNote: The phrase 'droppings of thy blood' is archaic poetic imagery. Explain redemption and cleansing from the cited KJV passages.

entries.title: Dissolve my heart in thankfulness
entries.text:
Thus might I hide my blushing face
While his dear cross appears,
Dissolve my heart in thankfulness,
And melt my eyes to tears.
entries.slideText:
Dissolve my heart in thankfulness,
And melt my eyes to tears.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed reflective stanza for Communion or a response to preaching on Christ's cross.
entries.reviewNote: Emotional response is not the measure of saving faith. Center the application on Christ's finished work and the cited KJV texts.

entries.title: Without thy presence, Lord
entries.text:
Nor earth nor all the sky
Can one delight afford;
No not a drop of real joy,
Without thy presence, Lord.
entries.slideText:
No not a drop of real joy,
Without thy presence, Lord.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed devotional stanza about the believer's highest joy being found in God.
entries.reviewNote: This is intense poetic expression, not a denial of God's common gifts. Interpret it through the cited KJV passages.

entries.title: Their conquest to the Lamb
entries.text:
I ask them whence their victory came,
They, with united breath,
Ascribe their conquest to the Lamb,
Their triumph to his death.
entries.slideText:
Ascribe their conquest to the Lamb,
Their triumph to his death.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed victory stanza after showing that the believer's triumph belongs to Christ.
entries.reviewNote: The pictured conversation with departed saints is poetic imagination. Ground the doctrine of victory in the cited KJV passages.
